t: Fix Product Name Format - Cleaning and Grouping Manual Sales Entries
o: Product names in Sales were typed by hand, so the same product can appear with stray spaces and random casing: LCPHONE, LCPhone and LcPhOnE are all one product. The task is to normalize every name to trimmed lowercase, bucket each sale into a month using the YYYY-MM form of sale_date, and count the sales per (product, month) pair. In the example, the three phone spellings collapse into lcphone with 2 sales in 2000-01 and 1 in 2000-02, while the two keychain spellings give lckeychain 2 sales in 2000-02. Because near-duplicate spellings must merge, the trimming and lowercasing have to happen in (or before) the GROUP BY, not after aggregation. The final ordering by product_name then sale_date ascending applies to those same normalized values.
k: Normalize before aggregating: LOWER(TRIM(product_name)) must be part of the grouping key, or variant spellings form separate groups.
DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m') converts a date into the monthly bucket string the output requires.
COUNT(*) after grouping yields the per-product-per-month totals; the ORDER BY then sorts by the cleaned name and month.

a.n: Approach 1: Normalize, format, and GROUP BY
a.i: Apply TRIM and LOWER to product_name directly in the SELECT list, convert sale_date to its YYYY-MM key with DATE_FORMAT, and GROUP BY both expressions so all manual-entry variants collapse into one row per product per month. COUNT(*) simply counts the raw sale rows inside each group. A final ORDER BY on the two cleaned columns satisfies the required ascending order with tie-breaking by month.
s: Trim and lowercase product_name; format sale_date as YYYY-MM.
GROUP BY those two cleaned expressions.
Count the rows of each group with COUNT(*) as total.
ORDER BY product_name, then sale_date, both ascending.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT
    LOWER(TRIM(product_name)) AS product_name,
    DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m') AS sale_date,
    COUNT(*) AS total
FROM Sales
GROUP BY product_name, sale_date
ORDER BY product_name, sale_date;
"""

a.t: O(n log n) - one scan to aggregate plus sorting the resulting groups.
a.sp: O(g) - one row per distinct cleaned (product_name, month) group.

a.n: Approach 2: Normalize in a subquery, aggregate outside
a.i: Project a derived table in which every row is already normalized to a cleaned name and month string, then run the aggregation over those tidy columns. It is slightly more verbose but separates cleaning logic from counting logic and makes it explicit that grouping operates on canonical values. This layout pays off when additional aggregates or filters reuse the same cleaned data.
s: Build a subquery emitting cleaned product_name and the formatted month.
Aggregate the derived table grouped by product_name and month.
Take COUNT(*) per group as total.

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem - Python driver not applicable.
# SQL solution:
"""
SELECT product_name,
       sale_month AS sale_date,
       COUNT(*) AS total
FROM (
    SELECT
        LOWER(TRIM(product_name)) AS product_name,
        DATE_FORMAT(sale_date, '%Y-%m') AS sale_month
    FROM Sales
) cleaned
GROUP BY product_name, sale_month
ORDER BY product_name, sale_month;
"""

a.t: O(n log n) - same scan-and-sort work as the direct grouping.
a.sp: O(n) - the materialized cleaned subquery of n rows.

w: Lead with the direct GROUP BY version in an interview; it is short, correct, and easy to defend. Mention the subquery layout only if asked to separate transformation from reporting. Pitfalls: forgetting TRIM or LOWER leaves duplicate-looking groups; grouping by the raw date while formatting only in the output splits a month in two; and remember the sort keys are the normalized values. Likely follow-ups: case-insensitive matching under a case-sensitive collation, adding yearly rollups, or handling names that differ by more than whitespace.
